pages.name: The back-emf coil
pages.text: An ideal coil of 31.8 mH on a 100 V peak, 50 Hz supply. Its [[flux]] grows and shrinks with its current. The short [[tangent]] rides the dashed current wave, and the coil's voltage, its [[back-emf]], is its inductance × the tangent's steepness. At 0 ms the current crosses zero at its steepest, so the voltage is at its 100 V peak. Drag the time cursor.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 2.5 ms the current is 7.07 A and the coil's voltage 70.7 V. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: At the top
pages.task: The cursor is parked at 5 ms, where the current is at its 10 A top. What is the coil's voltage at that instant?
pages.why: The coil's voltage follows how fast its current is changing, not how big it is. At its top the current has stopped rising and not yet started to fall, so for that instant it is not changing: the tangent lies flat and the voltage is 0 V. 100 V is a resistor's rule, the biggest current with the biggest voltage. −100 V comes at 10 ms, where the current falls fastest.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 5.0 ms the current is 10.00 A and the coil's voltage 0.0 V. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: A quarter cycle ahead
pages.text: Now the cursor sweeps one whole 20 ms cycle, tracing the voltage from the tangent: high where the current climbs steeply, zero where it tops out, low where it falls. Watch which wave reaches its top first. Drag the cursor to follow it.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 20.0 ms the current is 0.00 A and the coil's voltage 100.0 V. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: Which leads?
pages.task: Here are the coil's waves again, standing still. Which leads, and by how much?
pages.answer: The voltage, by a quarter cycle
pages.why: Read along the time axis. The voltage tops out at 20 ms and the current 5 ms later, at 25 ms. Whichever peaks first is ahead, so the voltage leads by 5 ms, a quarter of the 20 ms cycle, and the current lags by the same: the voltage [[leads]] and the current [[lags]]. Measured as the angle by which the voltage leads, the coil's [[phase angle]] is +90°. Reading the current's later peak as ahead turns it round. Half a cycle, 10 ms, would put the current's top where the voltage has its bottom.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 10 ohms.
options: The current, by a quarter cycle
The voltage, by half a cycle
The voltage, by a quarter cycle

pages.name: A faster supply
pages.text: The frequency plays from 50 Hz up to 100 Hz on the same 100 V peak. The back-emf must still match the supply, so at 0 ms the tangent stays just as steep, and in half the time the current climbs only half as high. The coil's opposition, the voltage ÷ the current, is its [[inductive reactance]], X_L. Now slide the frequency and the inductance, and try the two coils in the rows.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 100 V peak, 100 Hz. At 0.0 ms the current is 0.00 A and the coil's voltage 100.0 V. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 20 ohms.

pages.name: On board ship
pages.task: A marine college's notes (a secondary source) give 60 Hz as the frequency most common on board ship. With the same 100 V peak, how high does this coil's current peak at 60 Hz?
pages.why: X_L rises in step with the frequency: 10 Ω × 60 ÷ 50 = 12 Ω, the same as 2π × 60 × 0.0318. The supply's peak is still 100 V, so the current peaks at 100 ÷ 12 = 8.33 A. More frequency means more reactance and less current. 12 A scales the current up instead, and 10 A leaves the frequency out, as for a resistor.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 100 V peak, 60 Hz. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 12 ohms.

pages.name: Taking and giving back
pages.text: Back at 50 Hz, the power wave is the voltage × the current at each instant, as in lesson 3. While the current grows, the dot climbs: energy goes into the coil's field. While it dies away, the voltage turns negative and the dot dips: the energy comes back. Drag the cursor through a cycle and compare lesson 3's heater.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 10.0 ms the current is 0.00 A and the coil's voltage −100.0 V. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: Meter readings
pages.task: A meter on the coil reads 70.7 V and 7.07 A, the same as on lesson 3's heater. What power does the coil average?
pages.why: Volts × amps gives a heater's average power because its power never dips below zero. This coil's power dips below zero as far as it rises above: what it takes into its field in one quarter cycle, it hands back in the next. So it averages 0 W, although 70.7 × 7.07 is about 500. −500 W counts only the giving back.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: Down to steady DC
pages.text: Follow the X_L line down to 0 Hz, steady DC. There the current never changes, so the flux never changes and there is no back-emf: X_L is 0 Ω. Only the wire's own resistance is left, an example 0.5 Ω, and on a steady 100 V it lets through 100 ÷ 0.5 = 200 A. The coil pushes back against change, not against current.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: The ohmmeter
pages.task: An ohmmeter across this coil reads 0.5 Ω, yet on 50 Hz it opposes with 10 Ω. Why the difference?
pages.answer: The meter's steady current makes no back-emf
pages.why: An ohmmeter drives a small steady current. A steady current makes a steady flux, so there is no back-emf and the meter sees only the wire's 0.5 Ω, the 0 Hz end of the X_L line. On 50 Hz the current changes all the time, and the back-emf gives 10 Ω of reactance. A healthy coil reads like this too, so it is not shorted, and reactance follows the frequency, not the voltage.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 10 ohms.
options: Reactance only appears at high voltage
The meter's steady current makes no back-emf

pages.name: Mixed: a slower supply
pages.task: Mixed. The same coil goes on a 25 Hz supply with the same 100 V peak. What does its current do?
pages.why: Half the frequency halves the reactance: 10 Ω × 25 ÷ 50 = 5 Ω, so the current peaks at 100 ÷ 5 = 20 A. It still lags a quarter cycle, 10 ms at 25 Hz, because the voltage still peaks where the current is steepest, at any frequency. 5 A scales the wrong way, and an ideal coil's current is never in step with its voltage.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 100 V peak, 25 Hz. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 5 ohms.
options: 20 A, in step with the voltage

pages.name: Mixed: a mains coil
pages.task: Mixed. An ideal coil draws 4 A from 230 V, 50 Hz mains, so its X_L is 57.5 Ω. What does it draw on a 230 V, 60 Hz supply, and what power does it average?
pages.why: X_L rises with the frequency: 57.5 Ω × 60 ÷ 50 = 69 Ω, so the current is 230 ÷ 69 = 3.33 A. An ideal coil still takes energy into its field and hands it all back each quarter cycle, so it averages 0 W; a real coil's wire would take a few watts. 4.8 A scales the current up with the frequency, and 230 × 3.33 = 767 is volts × amps, which for a coil is not watts.
pages.alt: An ideal coil on 230 V, 60 Hz. The voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Its reactance is 69 ohms.
